posts.title: Why 70% of Manufacturing AI Projects Fail
posts.excerpt: Despite massive investments in artificial intelligence, the majority of manufacturing AI projects never reach production. The problem isn't the technology — it's the gap between data science teams and the shop floor. Most AI solutions are built in boardrooms, not on production lines. Here's what separates the 30% that succeed from the rest.
posts.content:
Manufacturing leaders across India are investing heavily in AI and Industry 4.0, expecting transformative results. Yet studies consistently show that 70% of these initiatives fail to move beyond pilot stages. The reasons are almost always the same: poor data quality, disconnected teams, and a fundamental misunderstanding of what AI can and cannot do in a production environment.

The root cause is that most AI projects are led by IT or data science teams who have limited exposure to the realities of the shop floor. They build models on historical data that may be incomplete, inconsistent, or simply wrong. Meanwhile, the operators and engineers who understand the process nuances are never meaningfully involved in the project. The result? A sophisticated model that fails when it encounters the variability of real manufacturing.

The firms that succeed treat AI as an operational tool, not a technology experiment. They start with a clearly defined business problem — reduced scrap, improved OEE, better demand forecasting — and work backward to the data and algorithms needed. They involve line supervisors and operators from day one. They run small, focused pilots on a single line or cell, prove the value, and then scale. Most importantly, they invest in change management and training alongside the technology.

At GroEdge, we help manufacturers bridge this gap. Our approach starts with operational readiness assessment — do you have the data infrastructure, the process discipline, and the people capability to actually benefit from AI? If not, we build those foundations first. Technology without operational excellence is just expensive decoration.
posts.author: Rajesh Pal

posts.title: Lean vs Industry 4.0: Why You Need Both
posts.excerpt: The debate between Lean manufacturing and Industry 4.0 is a false choice. Lean provides the operational discipline that makes digital tools effective. Industry 4.0 provides the visibility and speed that makes Lean sustainable at scale. Indian manufacturers who try to skip Lean and jump straight to digital will burn through capital with little to show for it.
posts.content:
There is a persistent myth in Indian manufacturing that Lean and Industry 4.0 are competing philosophies. Some firms have embraced Lean religiously for decades and view digital transformation with suspicion. Others see Industry 4.0 as the future and consider Lean a relic of a previous era. Both perspectives are wrong, and the cost of this misunderstanding is enormous.

Lean manufacturing provides the foundational discipline that every operation needs: standardised work, visual management, waste elimination, and a culture of continuous improvement. Without these, digital tools have nothing to optimise. You cannot automate a broken process and expect good results — you will simply produce defects faster. We see this repeatedly in firms that invest in MES, SCADA, or IoT platforms without first establishing basic process control.

Industry 4.0, on the other hand, provides capabilities that Lean alone cannot: real-time visibility across the entire value chain, predictive analytics that anticipate problems before they occur, and the ability to optimise across multiple variables simultaneously. These capabilities multiply the impact of Lean practices and make continuous improvement sustainable rather than dependent on individual champions.

The winning formula is what we call Operational Excellence 4.0 — Lean as the operating system, digital as the accelerator. Start with Lean to stabilise your processes, build discipline, and develop your people. Then layer on digital tools to enhance visibility, speed up feedback loops, and scale improvements. This is exactly the approach we take with our clients, and the results consistently outperform firms that try to do one or the other in isolation.
posts.author: Rajesh Pal

posts.title: How to Calculate Your True Cost of Poor Quality
posts.excerpt: Most Indian manufacturers dramatically underestimate their Cost of Poor Quality because they only count visible scrap and rework. The real COPQ — including warranty claims, customer churn, lost capacity, and managerial firefighting — is typically 15-25% of revenue. Here's a practical framework to uncover the hidden numbers and build a business case for quality improvement.
posts.content:
Ask any plant head in India about their cost of poor quality, and they will likely quote you a number between 2% and 4% of revenue. This figure usually represents only the most visible costs — scrap, rework, and reject materials. The true cost of poor quality, when you include all internal and external failure costs plus prevention and appraisal costs, is typically 15-25% of revenue. For a ₹500 crore plant, that represents ₹75-125 crore in annual losses.

The hidden costs are the ones that rarely appear on any P&L line item. When a production line stops due to a quality issue, the overtime needed to recover lost output is charged to the production budget, not the quality budget. When a customer complaint requires an engineering team to spend three days investigating root cause, those hours are absorbed into general overhead. When warranty claims spike, the cost is attributed to customer service, not manufacturing quality.

To calculate your true COPQ, start by categorising costs into three buckets: prevention costs (training, process design, supplier quality management), appraisal costs (inspection, testing, audits), and failure costs (internal failures like scrap and rework, and external failures like returns, warranty, and customer penalties). For each category, include both direct costs and the opportunity cost of capacity and resources consumed.

We recommend conducting a structured COPQ assessment at least annually. The exercise itself creates awareness and builds urgency for improvement. In our experience, firms that accurately understand their COPQ are 3-4 times more likely to secure investment approval for quality improvement initiatives. The numbers speak for themselves — you just have to know where to look.
posts.author: Rajesh Pal

posts.title: 5 Signs Your S&OP Process Is Broken
posts.excerpt: Sales and Operations Planning is the backbone of supply chain performance, yet many Indian manufacturers run a version of S&OP that is little more than a monthly meeting with spreadsheets. If your OTIF is below 80%, your inventory keeps growing while service levels drop, or your production team and sales team are constantly at odds, your S&OP process needs urgent attention.
posts.content:
Sales and Operations Planning should be the single most powerful process in any manufacturing organisation. It aligns demand and supply, balances capacity and inventory, and provides a clear roadmap for the next 12-18 months. Yet in our experience working with over 60 manufacturing facilities across India, the majority are running broken S&OP processes that create more problems than they solve.

Sign one: the monthly S&OP meeting is dominated by firefighting. Instead of looking forward, the team spends 80% of the time discussing why last month's numbers were wrong. Sign two: the demand plan and the production plan are fundamentally different documents that no one reconciles. Sales builds their forecast in one spreadsheet, production builds their plan in another, and the gap is bridged by expedited shipments and emergency overtime. Sign three: inventory keeps rising even as customer service levels decline — a classic symptom of poor S&OP.

Sign four: there is no single version of the truth. Every department operates on its own data, its own assumptions, and its own metrics. When the CEO asks about next quarter's capacity, three different people give three different answers. Sign five: no one outside the supply chain team owns the S&OP process. It is treated as a scheduling exercise rather than a strategic business management process.

Fixing S&OP requires both process redesign and cultural change. The process must be structured with clear weekly and monthly cadences, defined inputs and outputs, and executive-level decision-making forums. The cultural change requires breaking down the silos between sales, production, finance, and supply chain. At GroEdge, we have helped dozens of firms transform their S&OP from a spreadsheet exercise into a genuine competitive advantage.
posts.author: Rajesh Pal

posts.title: Supply Chain Resilience: Lessons from India's Pharma Corridor
posts.excerpt: India's pharmaceutical manufacturing corridor in Gujarat and Maharashtra has weathered global disruptions better than most supply chains worldwide. What can other industries learn from pharma's approach to supply chain resilience, dual sourcing, and regulatory-driven quality systems? The answer lies in building redundancy without excess cost.
posts.content:
When the global pandemic disrupted supply chains in unprecedented ways, India's pharmaceutical corridor demonstrated remarkable resilience. While other industries scrambled for alternatives, pharma manufacturers in Gujarat and Maharashtra largely maintained continuity. Understanding why reveals principles that every Indian manufacturer can apply.

The pharma industry's resilience is not accidental — it is the result of deliberate choices driven by decades of regulatory pressure. FDA and WHO requirements have forced pharma companies to maintain validated processes, dual-source critical materials, maintain safety stock for essential inputs, and build robust quality management systems. These compliance requirements, often seen as burdens, turned out to be the very capabilities that provided resilience during a crisis.

The key lesson is that resilience is not about holding massive inventory — it is about building operational capabilities that allow rapid adaptation. This includes strategic dual sourcing of critical materials, maintaining flexibility in production scheduling, investing in real-time supply chain visibility, and developing supplier relationships that go beyond transactional purchasing. Phrama firms also invest heavily in scenario planning and stress-testing their supply chains against various disruption models.

For Indian manufacturers in other sectors, the path to resilience starts with a critical assessment of your supply chain vulnerabilities. Where do you have single points of failure? Which inputs have long lead times? Which suppliers are financially or geographically concentrated? Once you map these risks, you can systematically address them through diversification, strategic inventory positioning, and capability building. The investment is modest compared to the cost of a major supply chain disruption.
posts.author: Rajesh Pal

posts.title: The Hidden Factory: Where 20-40% of Capacity Disappears
posts.excerpt: Every manufacturing plant has a hidden factory — the collection of undocumented workarounds, informal processes, and unrecorded losses that silently consume capacity. In most Indian plants, this hidden factory accounts for 20-40% of total capacity. Finding and eliminating it requires going beyond the official process maps and understanding how work actually happens on the floor.
posts.content:
The concept of the hidden factory was first described by quality guru Armand Feigenbaum, and it remains one of the most powerful frameworks for understanding manufacturing losses. The hidden factory represents all the activities in a plant that consume resources but are not captured in official processes, metrics, or systems. It is the gap between how you think your plant runs and how it actually runs.

In a typical Indian manufacturing plant, the hidden factory manifests in several ways. Operators develop unofficial workarounds to compensate for unreliable equipment, but these workarounds are never documented or measured. Supervisors make informal scheduling adjustments that create hidden bottlenecks downstream. Quality issues are addressed through undocumented inspection steps that add cycle time but appear in no process map. Maintenance activities are performed reactively, consuming capacity that should be available for production.

The cumulative impact is staggering. When we conduct operational audits at client facilities, we consistently find that 20-40% of theoretical capacity is consumed by hidden factory activities. For a plant running at 65% OEE, this means 10-20 percentage points of capacity are being lost to processes that no one tracks, measures, or understands.

Revealing the hidden factory requires a structured approach. Start with detailed time studies and process observation at every workstation. Map the official process flow alongside the actual process flow, and document every deviation. Implement real-time loss tracking at every production cell. Most importantly, create a culture where operators and supervisors feel safe to report problems without fear of blame. The hidden factory thrives in cultures of silence and blame. When you create transparency, the hidden losses become visible, and the path to improvement becomes clear.
posts.author: Rajesh Pal

posts.title: BRSR Compliance: What Indian Manufacturers Need to Know
posts.excerpt: India's Business Responsibility and Sustainability Reporting framework is moving from voluntary to mandatory for listed companies, and the ripple effects will reach unlisted manufacturers through supply chain requirements. Understanding BRSR early gives Indian manufacturers a competitive advantage and prevents last-minute scrambles that compromise data quality.
posts.content:
The Business Responsibility and Sustainability Reporting framework, introduced by SEBI, is reshaping how Indian companies approach environmental, social, and governance disclosures. Initially mandatory only for the top 1000 listed companies by market capitalisation, the scope is expanding, and the impact is already being felt throughout manufacturing supply chains. Even unlisted manufacturers are finding that their large listed customers are requiring ESG data and compliance documentation as a condition of doing business.

For Indian manufacturers, BRSR compliance is not just a reporting exercise — it requires genuine operational changes. The framework demands quantitative data on energy consumption, water usage, waste generation, greenhouse gas emissions, employee safety metrics, diversity indicators, and community impact. Many manufacturers, particularly SMEs, do not currently have the systems to collect, validate, and report this data consistently.

The practical challenges are significant. Most Indian manufacturing plants track energy consumption at the facility level, not at the process or product level. Water and waste data is often estimated rather than measured. Safety metrics may be recorded in inconsistent formats across different shifts and locations. Building the data infrastructure for BRSR compliance requires investment in metering, tracking systems, and reporting processes.

The firms that start now will have a significant advantage. Early investment in data infrastructure not only ensures compliance but also reveals operational improvement opportunities. Energy data, when collected at a granular level, often reveals 10-15% reduction opportunities. Waste tracking drives reduction initiatives. Safety data, when properly analysed, enables proactive risk mitigation. At GroEdge, we help manufacturers build ESG data infrastructure that serves both compliance requirements and operational improvement goals simultaneously.
posts.author: Rajesh Pal

posts.title: Building a Supervisor Academy: The Missing Link in Digital Transformation
posts.excerpt: Indian manufacturers spend crores on ERP, MES, and IoT platforms, but rarely invest in the frontline supervisors who are supposed to use these tools daily. The result is expensive systems that sit underutilised while the shop floor continues to run on instinct and experience. A structured Supervisor Academy bridges this gap and accelerates digital transformation adoption.
posts.content:
The frontline supervisor is the most important person in any manufacturing transformation, and the most neglected. Companies invest millions in technology platforms, hire consultants for strategy, and train managers on new processes — but the supervisors who actually run the shop floor are expected to figure it out on their own. This is the single biggest reason digital transformation projects stall in Indian manufacturing.

The typical Indian manufacturing supervisor has 10-15 years of shop floor experience, deep process knowledge, and strong people skills. What they typically lack is comfort with digital tools, data-driven decision making, and structured problem-solving methodologies. They know the process intuitively but struggle to articulate or teach it. They manage by walking around but cannot translate observations into actionable digital insights. They are excellent at firefighting but have never been trained to prevent fires.

A properly designed Supervisor Academy addresses these gaps through a structured curriculum that blends operational excellence fundamentals with digital literacy. The programme should cover visual management, standardised work, data collection and analysis, root cause problem solving, and the specific digital tools the organisation is deploying. Critically, it must be practical — classroom theory alone does not change behaviour on the shop floor.

At GroEdge, our Supervisor Academy programmes typically run for 12-16 weeks, combining classroom sessions with on-the-job coaching. Supervisors learn by doing — they identify real problems in their own areas, apply structured methodologies, and use the digital tools to track and sustain improvements. The ROI is dramatic: firms that invest in supervisor capability typically see 25-40% improvement in digital tool adoption, 15-20% improvement in team productivity, and significant reduction in supervisor turnover. The missing link in your digital transformation might be sitting right on your shop floor.
posts.author: Rajesh Pal
